title: Camera: Light Into Numbers
description: Component lesson. Zoom in far enough on any photo and the picture disappears — all that's left is a grid of numbers.

content.value: Every sensor so far in this course reports one number: a distance, a HIGH or LOW, a temperature. A camera is different — it's really thousands of tiny light sensors packed onto one chip, each reporting its own number, all at once.

Light passes through a lens and lands on a grid of light-sensitive spots called pixels. Each pixel measures how much red, green and blue light hit it, and reports three numbers, 0 to 255 each — that's what "RGB" means. Zoom out far enough and thousands of these tiny coloured squares blend into what looks like a smooth photo.

content.title: 🔍 Zoom in
content.hint: Drag zoom all the way up, then click individual pixels to read their RGB numbers.

content.value: Once a picture is just numbers, a computer can do real work on it, in stages: capture the raw grid, resize it smaller for speed, sometimes convert it to grayscale (throwing away colour to simplify the numbers further), then look for patterns — and finally decide something based on what it found.

Resolution is exactly this trade-off made explicit: more pixels means more detail, but also more numbers a controller has to process every single frame. A small ESP32 camera module often deliberately captures fewer pixels than your phone, on purpose, to keep up.
Key takeaway: a camera is a grid of tiny sensors, each reporting an RGB number. A picture is nothing more than that grid of numbers — everything a computer does with an image starts from there.

quiz.question: What does a single camera pixel actually report?
options: A description of what object it's looking at
Three numbers — how much red, green and blue light hit it
A single brightness value only, always
quiz.explain: RGB stands for exactly this: three separate light measurements per pixel, each 0–255.

quiz.question: Why might a camera pipeline convert an image to grayscale before further processing?
options: To make the picture look nicer
To reduce each pixel to one number instead of three, simplifying and speeding up the processing that follows
Grayscale is required by law for robots
quiz.explain: Throwing away colour when it isn't needed cuts the data a controller has to process by two-thirds — a real, practical trade-off.

quiz.question: Why might a small robot's camera deliberately capture fewer pixels than a modern phone?
options: More pixels means more numbers to process every frame, and a small controller can only keep up with so much
Fewer pixels always look identical to more
quiz.explain: Resolution trades detail for processing load — a deliberate choice matched to what the controller can handle in real time.
